newsitem.title: HUNGARY: ANTENNA HUNGARIA SELL-OFF DYING SLOWLY - ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: ANTENNA HUNGARIA SELL-OFF DYING SLOWLY - ANALYSTS.

text.p: Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn's recent comments that his government has no plans to sell broadcaster Antenna Hungaria signals the privatisation is off for the foreseeable future, analysts and investors said on Tuesday.
Horn said last week the government had no plans to privatise Antenna Hungaria Rt, which transmits all of Hungary's national television and radio programmes.
"Privatising Antenna Hungaria is not on the government's agenda," Horn told reporters.
Media analyst Attila Ledenyi said that in practical terms the question is unlikely to be raised again until the privatisation of Hungary's media is settled late in 1997.
"A compromise was made a couple of months ago within the government not to deal with Antenna Hungaria until after the radio and TV frequencies are given out," he said.
"That means not until at least the second half of 1997."
The media sell-off involves the state-owned second channel and a third channel using a currently unused frequency.
Two national radio frequencies are also available.

Hungary's media law, passed last December after four years of bitter political dispute, stipulated 10-year concessions for the two television channels should be put out to tender in time for the new channels to be launched on January 1.
However, government policy changes and uncertainties over Antenna Hungaria, which will upgrade the third frequency to cover the whole of Hungary, have caused the process to fall way behind schedule.

The strongest opposition to the sale of Antenna Hungaria, which is owed 2.5 billion forints in unpaid broadcasting fees by Hungary's national radio and television channels, comes from Mihaly Revesz, chairman of the national broadcasting authority ORTT, which is overseeing the media privatisation.
Revesz, a close ally of premier Horn, is opposed on political grounds to allowing the physical means of broadcasting programmes as well as the channels themselves to fall into foreign ownership.
Such is Revesz's political sway that his views could eventually kill the sale all together, Ledenyi said.
"It could be the case that they drop the idea of privatising because of strong lobbying from Revesz," he said.
"The story may be over but if they think so they haven't made it public."

One reason for not making public a decision to cancel the sale is that the government is bound by a March decree to privatise Antenna Hungaria and could provoke a row with its coalition partners the Free Democrats, who favour the sale, if it moves to cancel the law.

France's Telediffusion de France was the only bidder in the state privatisation energy's (APV) original tender to sell 50 percent plus one share of Antenna Hungaria was turned down as it was well below the 8.4-billion-forint asking price.
The APV announced its intention to declare a new tender in June but said it had postponed the deal.
TDF remained interested in the company but by September, with no word on a new sale, decided to close its office.

"We closed our office because we were waiting for a clarification of the government's real intent," Jean-Francois Fenech, business development manager for TDF's international division, told Reuters "It was an economic decision."
"We are still interested because we have been cooperating with the firm for five years -- but under reasonable conditions," he said.
GTS Hungary, a member subsidiary of Global TeleSystems systems of the U.S., was also rumoured to be interested entering the bidding in the second tender.
"We were not really ready for the first tender but we would have been interested in the conditions for the second," GTS Hungary's managing director Istvan Pesti told reporters last week.
But Pesti said he was not very hopeful that such a tender will now take place.
"If you ask me I don't believe the company is going to be privatised in the near future," he told Reuters.
